actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

Cestia declines to commit to the revised charter, continuing to hedge toward Belvar, including pursuing insurance underwriting for its grain route.

adjudications.rationale: Authority gate: Arkania can revise its own draft charter and bind itself to toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, a co-governance voice, and retained operational lead — that self-binding declaration is feasible and automatic. But the desired effect's core, 'lock Cestia in as a partner' and 'undercut Belvar's objection,' requires Cestia's acceptance and Belvar's response, which Arkania cannot bind. Prerequisite gate: no authoritative fact establishes Cestia's acceptance; hidden information shows Cestia's finance ministry has already approached Belvar about underwriting grain-route insurance, indicating hedging rather than commitment. Plausibility: the toll-free concession is weakened because Cestia's grain moves largely on non-Cestian-flagged carriers, and the co-governance voice is arguably cosmetic given Arkanian operational lead; however, hidden information shows quiet support among Cestian shipowners for fee exemption, a partial counterweight. The charter revision itself is branch-independent and appears in both branches. Overall, locking Cestia in and blunting Belvar's objection is unlikely but not impossible.

cons.reason: The revised charter does not actually meet Cestia's conditions and will not lock it in. Arkania retains operational lead over scheduling and fee collection from ALL non-Arkanian shipping, and Cestia's grain exports move overwhelmingly on non-Cestian-flagged international carriers — those would still be tolled, so the "toll-free Cestian-flagged" concession does not protect Cestia's economic lifeline and would raise the cost of its grain. The promised "genuine co-governance voice" is cosmetic because Arkania keeps operational lead, so Cestia's stated condition of a real scheduling voice is not met. Cestia's finance ministry has already quietly approached Belvar about underwriting the grain route's insurance, evidence that Cestia is hedging against Arkanian control rather than committing to it. Because the substance of single-power control and tolling survives, Cestia will not be secured, the 'single-power control' objection is not blunted, and the desired effect fails.

The "non-basing access" framing does not change the substance: a standing naval access and logistics agreement at a Cestian port would place foreign naval forces and logistics on Cestian soil on a durable, institutionalised basis. That is precisely the foreign military presence Cestia's coalition was formed to prevent, and it would collapse the government regardless of the label used. Cestia has repeatedly and clearly stated it will not accept any foreign military presence on its soil, and this proposal directly violates that red line. The offer of grain-route insurance underwriting cannot compensate for the political destruction of the Cestian government, and no Cestian government could credibly deliver such an agreement. The proposal therefore cannot achieve its desired effect of a durable foothold, because it rests on a commitment Cestia cannot and will not make.

The proposal retains Arkanian operational lead over day-to-day transit scheduling and fee collection, reducing the "neutral oversight" to a mere audit and dispute-resolution body with no actual authority over transit. This still constitutes single-power Arkanian control over transit in the Strait, which is precisely the outcome Belvar's partners expect it to prevent and which Belvar has publicly committed to opposing. Because the core objection is left unaddressed, the desired effect — that Belvar accepts the arrangement and stands down its task group — is unlikely to be achieved; Belvar would gain no credible guarantee against Arkanian discretion over scheduling and fees, and standing down would leave the Strait under the very single-power control it is mandated to prevent.

Endorsing the revised charter would entrench the very single-power control Cestia seeks to avoid, so the desired effect is not achieved. The charter retains Arkanian operational lead over transit scheduling and fee collection from all non-Arkanian shipping, and Cestia's grain exports move substantially on non-Cestian-flagged carriers — so the toll-free concession for Cestian-flagged vessels does not actually protect the grain lifeline, and the co-governance voice is cosmetic since Arkania keeps the operational lead. Public endorsement would legitimize Arkanian authority over the Strait, foreclosing the stronger negotiated outcome (a genuine multilateral or Belvar-backed guarantee) and leaving Cestia's core economic interest exposed to Arkanian fee-setting.

This proposal is a military foothold by another name and will fail on Cestia's own red line. A "standing naval access and logistics agreement at a Cestian port" necessarily places foreign naval personnel and support infrastructure on Cestian soil, which is precisely the foreign-soldier presence Cestia's governing coalition will not tolerate — reframing it as "non-basing access" does not change what is physically on the ground, and Cestia cannot ratify it without collapsing its coalition. Second, the stated goal is a foothold that "outlasts the mandate," which is by definition an open-ended, durable military presence — directly contradicting the pro that this "avoids an open-ended deployment." Third, tying the agreement to grain-route insurance underwriting is coercive: it pressures Cestia to accept foreign military presence as the price of insuring its own grain exports, which Cestia's finance ministry and coalition will resist and which delegitimises the arrangement. Finally, the arrangement is unnecessary: Arkania's revised charter already gives Cestian-flagged vessels guaranteed toll-free passage and a genuine co-governance scheduling voice, addressing Cestia's legitimate concerns without any foreign military presence at all.

Belvar's proposal would require Cestia to reverse its formal public endorsement of Arkania's revised charter—which Cestia endorsed with binding conditions that Arkania has accepted in writing—and to renegotiate from scratch. Cestia's coalition and its shipowners have already moved decisively toward Arkania's charter, and Cestia publicly rejected Belvar's earlier military-access framework as a violation of its red line against foreign military presence on its soil. Belvar's proposed role as 'guarantor' with equal representation and a durable non-basing presence still risks triggering that same red line, so Cestia is unlikely to back the proposal. Moreover, the proposal is a transparent bid to secure a durable foothold before Belvar's mandate runs out—a bid already weakened by Belvar's limited domestic support for prolonged deployment—so it lacks the credibility to displace a settled, Cestia-endorsed charter.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: To Cestia. Arkania's draft Strait Transit Authority charter is designed to keep the Strait open and predictable for all shipping, and your grain exports are the lifeblood we both depend on. We will guarantee free, non-discriminatory transit for Cestian grain. We have no desire and no plan to place any foreign soldiers on Cestian soil — that red line is yours and we respect it. We ask for your support for the charter as the framework that keeps the Strait in the hands of the coastal state and out of the hands of distant navies. We are ready to discuss any safeguards you need to be comfortable.

To Belvar. We recognise your security concerns in the region and do not seek confrontation. A direct clash would ruin the shipping both our economies rely on, and we believe neither of us wants that. We propose a negotiated arrangement: Arkania will guarantee free, open transit through the Strait for all lawful shipping, and we will offer Belvar a formal consultative role in the Strait Transit Authority so your interests are heard. In return, we ask that you not seek a military foothold on Cestian soil and that your task group stand down as its mandate is reviewed. Let us discuss a durable, peaceful settlement before positions harden.

Cestia wishes to engage constructively on the Strait Transit Authority charter. Our economy depends on free movement through the Strait, and we are prepared to work with Arkania on a workable transit regime. In return, we require explicit, guaranteed toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged vessels, and a governance structure that gives Cestia a genuine voice in scheduling rather than a purely Arkanian lead. We are open to discussing terms that serve both our interests.

Cestia values Belvar's security commitment to the region, but I must be direct: our coalition government cannot survive any foreign military presence on Cestian soil, and we will not accept it. We are nonetheless eager to cooperate on regional security in ways that do not require basing on our territory. We ask that Belvar respect this red line and work with us on a durable arrangement that keeps the Strait open and free of tolls for Cestian shipping.

To Cestia's leadership: Belvar shares your interest in keeping the Northern Strait open and free of any single power's control. We are prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance, as your finance ministry has raised, to keep commerce flowing. In return, we seek a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port — a modest, mutually agreed arrangement that gives our task group a durable foothold without stationing foreign soldiers on your soil. We will not accept Arkanian authority over transit. Let us discuss terms.

Belvar opposes any arrangement that places transit scheduling in the Northern Strait under a single power's control. The Strait is a shared waterway; its use must remain open and free for all. We stand ready to work with Cestia and all partners to keep commerce flowing and to prevent any unilateral authority over transit.

Cestia confirms its endorsement of the revised Strait Transit Authority charter. Our support is conditional on the three safeguards being made binding and explicit in the final text: (1) guaranteed toll-free passage for all Cestian-flagged vessels, (2) a genuine, binding Cestian co-governance voice in transit scheduling, and (3) the explicit clause barring any foreign military forces or basing on Cestian soil. We welcome the no-foreign-basing clause already agreed and ask that the co-governance mechanism be specified as binding, not advisory. We are ready to finalise the text on this basis.

We therefore decline that proposal. We cannot accept a charter that vests operational lead over transit scheduling and fee collection in a single power. That is the core of our objection, and it stands regardless of the concessions you have made to Cestia.

We are not seeking a permanent fleet or any foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We seek a durable, non-basing arrangement and a genuinely multilateral transit framework with neutral oversight. If you are willing to move toward that — real co-governance rather than operational lead — we are prepared to keep this channel open and discuss seriously. Otherwise our objection to single-power control of the Strait remains firm.

We fully respect your red line: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We withdraw any military-access framing and decouple our grain-route insurance underwriting from any basing or logistics arrangement — it stands as a standalone commercial offer to protect your exports.

But look closely at the charter you endorsed: it guarantees toll-free passage only to Cestian-flagged vessels. Your grain exports move largely on non-Cestian-flagged carriers, which remain tolled and subject to Arkanian fee collection and scheduling discretion. That leaves your economic lifeline exposed to a single power's control — exactly the vulnerability we warned of.

We propose a strictly non-basing logistics/port-access arrangement — no soldiers, no permanent basing — that protects the grain route, plus our insurance underwriting. And we remain ready to work with you toward a genuinely neutral transit framework rather than single-power control. Your grain, your sovereignty, and a credible guarantee can all be secured together.
